items.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
items.summary: Interviews with 17 scientists reveal what they want to verify, safeguard, and keep under human control when using AI agents in research.
items.content:
Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
 November 25, 2026
 Ai2 

 Share 

 Tech Report 

 Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.
 These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.
 To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.
 Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.
 One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.
 Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.
 A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.
 Helping researchers check the work
 For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.
 But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.
 Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.
 But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.
 Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.
 These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.
 These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.
 Keep scientific judgment in the loop
 Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?
 An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”
 Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.
 Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.
 Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.
 Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.
 These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.
 The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.
 Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.
 This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.
 Build AI agents alongside scientists
 Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.
 Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of d

Simulation / Modeling / Design 

 How to Optimize NVFP4 Attention on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell Through Register Recycling

 Nov 25, 2026

 By Atharva Joshi 

 Like

 Discuss (0)

 L 

 T 

 F 

 R 

 E 

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVFP4 enables hardware-accelerated 4-bit matrix multiplication on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell GPUs, offering higher Tensor Core throughput than BF16 for attention workloads.
 An optimized SageAttention3 kernel splits each N128 score tile into two N64 register slots, reusing registers after softmax quantization to overlap the next tile's QK computation with the current tile's remaining operations.
 This register-recycling schedule reduces Tensor Core idle time without allocating a second full score buffer, improving NVFP4 attention kernel latency by up to 1.64x on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
 Reactor integrated the optimized kernel into its production serving stack for world models, achieving end-to-end inference latency reductions of up to 15.34% across LongLive, Helios, OmniDreams, and Cosmos 3 Nano workloads.
 The core optimization has been merged into the FlashInfer main branch for broader adoption.
 Next Steps
 Clone the FlashInfer main branch with its submodules and follow the source installation guide.
 Integrate the SM120 NVFP4 attention API into supported attention layers on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell and compare end-to-end latency and output quality against a BF16 baseline.
 Read Integrating NVF4 Attention into Real-Time Models on Reactor to learn how Reactor deployed this kernel for real customer traffic.

 Attention can be a major bottleneck when serving world foundation models , where long sequences make inference computationally demanding. On NVIDIA Hopper and NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs, FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention4 improve attention performance by overlapping matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) operations through softmax within a thread block.

 However, these hardware-specific pipelines cannot be applied directly to the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series (SM120), which uses a different Tensor Core architecture. For video generation models using BF16 inference, attention remains primarily MMA-bound on NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPUs, while softmax is a major bottleneck in forward attention on Blackwell data center GPUs.

 Introduced with NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, NVFP4 offers hardware-accelerated 4-bit matrix multiplication, enabling higher Tensor Core throughput and creating an opportunity to accelerate attention beyond BF16. But sustaining high throughput requires careful coordination of softmax, data movement, and intermediate storage. Dependencies between these stages can leave Tensor Cores idle, limiting how effectively the kernel uses the available compute.

 This post explains how to accelerate NVFP4 attention on the SM120 architecture through register recycling and improved scheduling. By reclaiming score registers after the softmax outputs have been packed into NVFP4, the next tile’s matrix multiplication can overlap with remaining softmax work on the current tile. This creates a more efficient pipeline that reduces Tensor Core idle time and improves utilization without requiring a second full score buffer.

 Reactor , a developer platform that provides global low-latency infrastructure and APIs for deploying and scaling real-time video, robotics, and world models, integrated this kernel in their production serving stack to serve real customer traffic and saw tremendous speedups. Their benchmarks are shared in this post.

 Improving throughput with NVFP4 

 NVIDIA RTX Blackwell has lower BF16 matmul throughput compared to the data center variants. While data center workloads are bounded by softmax (FlashAttention4 tries to solve this through pipelining and exp2 emulation), the NVIDIA RTX Blackwell is bounded by MMA on BF16 Attention. Due to higher TFLOP/s for NVFP4, throughput can be improved to achieve better performance.

 Attention compute 

 The general attention computation and the two core matrix multiplications it involves are:

 Query-Key matrix multiplication (\(QK\)) : The first matmul in attention, \(QKᵀ\), where \(Q\) contains query vectors and \(K\) contains key vectors. It computes the attention scores used by softmax.

 Attention-Weight Value matrix multiplication (\(PV\)) : The second matmul in attention, \(PV\), where \(P\) contains softmax-derived attention weights and \(V\) contains value vectors. It combines the value vectors according to their attention weights to produce the output. In the tiled attention kernel discussed here, \(P\) contains unnormalized softmax weights, and final normalization is applied after the output has been accumulated across tiles (similar to FlashAttention).

 How SageAttention3 accelerates attention using NVFP4 

 SageAttention3 is a native NVFP4 attention mechanism specifically designed for NVIDIA RTX Blackwell streaming multiprocessor (SM) 120. It performs both \(QK\) and \(PV\) using NVFP4​. Its primary innovation came from performing two-level scaling for \(P\).​

 NVFP4 quantization generates two tensors: an NVFP4 data tensor and an FP8 scaling tensor. Because ​softmax outputs are bound to a narrow [0, 1] range, they can underutilize the NVFP4 dynamic range, resulting in accuracy degradation. Two-level scaling addresses this by first normalizing the values to fully utilize dynamic range before quantizing the result.

 SageAttention3 cooperative thread array stable state design 

 The SageAttention3 cooperative thread array (CTA) design is as follows:

 The CTA uses four producer warps and eight consumer warps. For each N128 tile, consumers execute \(QK\), softmax and probability quantization, and \(PV\) in sequence.

 While consumers perform softmax, scaling, and quantization, tensor-core activity has gaps. Video 1 illustrates this sequential execution.

# Current SageAttention 3 CTA Execution (per N tile)
# CTA Structure: 12 warps total (4 Producer, 8 Consumer)

For each N tile:
 # 1. Producer Role: Data Loading
 # Q is loaded once per M tile
 AsyncLoad(Q)
 # K, V, Scale Factors, and delta_s use 3-stage async TMA pipeline
 AsyncLoad(K, V, Scale_Factors, delta_s)

 # 2. Consumer Role: Dependency Chain (Serial Execution)
 # 8 Consumer warps (256-thread MMA collective)

 # A. QK Computation
 Execute_QK_OMMA()
 Apply_delta_s_correction()

 # B. Softmax & Quantization
 Apply_Masking()
 Execute_Online_Softmax()
 Execute_NVFP4_Probability_Quantization()

 # C. PV Computation
 Execute_PV_OMMA()

 # Note: Execution is strictly serial per N tile
 # No overlapping or independent fragments in flight

 The following observations can be drawn from this CTA design and the parallel thread execution (PTX) and instruction set architecture (ISA) for NVIDIA RTX Blackwell GPUs:

 First, TMA Loads are bound to Shapes of 128×128, not utilizing the entire shape would mean underutilizing our GPU bandwidth.

 Second, the NVIDIA Blackwell RTX OMMA operation remains constrained to m16, n8, k64 (where m and n represent LHS/RHS free dimensions, while k is the contraction axis), as specified by the PTX instruction mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale.scale_vec::4X.m16n8k64 .​

 To cover the full contraction dimension of k=128, two MMA instructions with k=64 must be issued. The current CTA design issues these instructions for \(QK\) in succession. Because MMA execution is synchronous, the issuing consumer warps wait for completion before proceeding to online softmax and intermediate quantization.

 This means that the operations within the stable loop are sequentially pipelined. There is a large gap in MMA activity, as there is no compute scheduled on the tensor cores. The warps are busy computing the softmax, scaling, and quantization operations.

 Video 1 shows the attention-kernel timeline, including sequential \(QK\) matrix multiplication, softmax, and \(PV\) matrix multiplication.

 Video 1. CTA timeline for original CTA design of SageAttention3 

 Register constraints

 Producer warps use 3,072 registers, and consumer warps use 59,392 registers. The total of 62,464 registers occupies approximately 95.3% of the SM’s register capacity. This leaves little room to hold an additional score tile while processing the current tile.

 Optimized CTA design

 The design retains four producer warps, eight consumer warps, and complete N128 K/V tile loads. The change is in how consumers compute and store attention scores. Each N128 score tile is split into two N64 halves, and each occupies a separate register slot.

 After one half has been exponentiated and quantized, its score registers are reused to compute the corresponding \(QK\) half of the next tile. This interleaves the next tile’s \(QK\) to work with the current tile’s remaining softmax, quantization, and \(PV\) operations.

 The online-softmax state is still updated across the complete N128 score tile before either half is consumed.

 Video 2 shows how this schedule fills gaps in tensor-core activity without allocating a second complete score tile.

 Video 2. CTA Timeline for optimized SageAttention3 

 The following pseudocode illustrates the optimized schedule, including the initial score computation, steady-state register reuse, and processing of the final tile.

 Unlike the original design, which completes \(QK\), softmax, quantization, and \(PV\) sequentially for each N128 tile, the optimized design splits the score tile into two N64 register slots. When half is quantized, its score registers are reused for the next tile’s \(QK\) computation. This allows work from adjacent tiles to be interleaved without allocating a second complete score tile, while retaining the same four producer warps and eight consumer warps.
